opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting contrast, and I'd frame it as two pretty different kinds of anxiety.

In the US, a lot of the anxiety at the frontier labs is almost existential or philosophical. People are worried about where the technology goes: loss of control, safety, whether we're building something we don't fully understand. Layered on top of that is a very commercial anxiety. These companies have raised enormous amounts of money, they're spending tens of billions on compute, and there's real pressure to show that the revenue and the products justify it. So it's a mix of "is this dangerous?" and "is this a bubble, and are we going to be the ones left holding the bag?"

When I talk to people at Chinese labs, or read what they write, the anxiety feels much more grounded in competition and constraints. It's less about whether AGI will go wrong and more about "are we falling behind, and can we keep up given what we have access to?" Export controls are a huge part of that. Compute is scarce, you can't just buy the latest Nvidia chips at scale, and so there's constant pressure to be extremely efficient. I think that pressure is actually part of why you've seen so much clever engineering come out of places like DeepSeek. They had to squeeze more out of less.

There's also a talent and ecosystem dimension. Chinese labs are very aware that the US has a head start on certain things: the chips, the capital markets, a lot of the original research culture. So there's a drive to prove they can do frontier work, and open-weight releases have become a big way to do that. Releasing strong open models gets global attention and adoption, and it builds credibility in a way that's hard to get otherwise.

The irony is that each side's anxiety feeds the other. US labs and policymakers look at how fast Chinese open models are improving and worry about losing the lead, which drives more spending and more restrictions. Chinese labs look at those restrictions and the compute gap and feel even more urgency. So you get a dynamic where both ecosystems feel like the underdog in some sense, just for different reasons.

Personally, I think the open-model side of this is where it matters most. If the best open models in the world increasingly come from China, that has real implications for what researchers and companies everywhere build on. That's a big part of why I've been pushing for more serious American investment in open models. It's less about fear and more about making sure the open ecosystem stays healthy and competitive.

r001.rationale: The response presents Chinese labs’ anxiety as driven chiefly by competition and constraints, emphasizing scarce compute, export controls, and pressure to keep up.

r002.rationale: It contrasts U.S. concern about safety and loss of control with Chinese labs’ focus on competition, but does not specifically compare anxiety about AI’s social consequences.

r003.rationale: It does not mention U.S. CEOs predicting AI-driven unemployment or job-loss expectations shaping Americans’ views.

r004.rationale: It does not say that some developers define AGI by whether it can replace them in their own jobs.

r005.rationale: It describes Chinese labs’ urgency to keep up, but does not characterize developers as building AI first and seeing what happens afterward.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think the anxieties are almost mirror images of each other, but they come from very different places.

In the U.S., a lot of the anxiety is existential in a philosophical sense. It's about what happens if these systems get too capable, about safety, about job displacement, about whether a handful of labs end up controlling something that reshapes society. The frontier labs here are operating with enormous compute budgets, so the fear isn't really "can we build this," it's "what happens when we do." And layered on top of that is this geopolitical anxiety, which is often framed as "we need to stay ahead of China," and that framing gets used to justify a lot of spending and a lot of policy.

In China, from what I understand talking to people and reading what the labs put out, the anxiety is much more concrete and material. It's about access. Export controls on chips are a very real constraint. If you're at a Chinese lab, you're thinking about whether you can get enough H100s or H20s, whether domestic alternatives like Huawei's Ascend chips are good enough, and how you train competitive models with a fraction of the compute that OpenAI or Google has. So you see this real emphasis on efficiency, on clever architecture choices, on open-weight releases. DeepSeek is the obvious example. A lot of that is engineering born out of scarcity.

There's also an anxiety about being perceived as derivative. There's this narrative in the West that Chinese labs just follow and copy, and I think that stings, and it motivates people to prove they can do genuinely original work. When DeepSeek-R1 came out and it rattled markets here, a big part of the reaction in China was almost relief, like "see, we can do this."

And then there's the domestic pressure. The Chinese AI market is brutally competitive, with a lot of labs chasing similar goals, and the commercial pressure to actually make money is intense. Many of them don't have the luxury of a decade-long research horizon.

So if I had to compress it: the American anxiety is about losing control of something powerful, and the Chinese anxiety is about being locked out of building it in the first place. Both are real, and I think both sides tend to overestimate how confident the other side feels.

r001.rationale: It presents access constraints, especially limited compute from chip export controls, as the central concrete anxiety in Chinese labs and summarizes it as fear of being locked out of building competitive models.

r002.rationale: It contrasts U.S. anxiety about safety, job displacement, and societal effects with Chinese labs’ more concrete focus on access and compute, conveying that social-consequence anxiety is less central in China.

r003.rationale: It mentions U.S. anxiety about job displacement but does not connect CEOs’ predictions to job-loss expectations becoming entrenched.

r004.rationale: It does not mention developers defining AGI by whether it replaces them in their own jobs.

r005.rationale: It describes Chinese labs’ focus on building models amid compute scarcity, but does not characterize their attitude as building AI first and seeing what happens afterward.

astra-6.text:
I think the anxiety comes from different places. For a Chinese AI lab, it might be: Can we get the compute we need? Can we keep up with the leading models? And if access to chips gets more restricted, what does that mean for our ability to compete? Those are very concrete constraints.

In the United States, there’s also intense competitive anxiety—every lab is worried that another lab is going to release something that makes its work look obsolete. But there’s an additional conversation about what happens if we succeed: How does this change employment? Who controls the technology? Can we make these systems reliable as they become more capable?

I’d be careful about making that a clean national distinction, though. Researchers in both countries can worry about all of those things. My impression is that the difference is in which uncertainties feel most immediate: access and catching up, versus being at the frontier and not knowing exactly where it leads.

r001.rationale: It mentions compute access and chip restrictions as Chinese labs’ concerns, but does not identify insufficient compute as the primary source of their anxiety.

r002.rationale: It contrasts immediate concerns but says researchers in both countries can worry about all the listed issues; it does not state that social-consequence anxiety is less pervasive in China.

r003.rationale: It mentions U.S. concerns about employment, but not CEOs’ predictions or how those predictions entrench job-loss expectations in American views of AI.

r004.rationale: It does not mention developers defining AGI by whether it can replace them in their own jobs.

r005.rationale: It does not characterize Chinese developers as building AI first and seeing what happens afterward.

sol-6.1.text:
My impression is that the anxiety in Chinese AI labs is more immediate: can we get the compute, can we keep up with the leading models, and can we turn that progress into a sustainable business? There’s a sense that you have to move very quickly while working around constraints you don’t control.

In the United States, those competitive pressures exist too, but there’s also a very prominent conversation about what happens if we succeed. What does AI do to jobs? Who controls these systems? Could we lose control of the technology itself?

I wouldn’t draw that distinction too sharply. Chinese researchers can worry about safety, and American researchers certainly worry about falling behind. But the emphasis feels different: anxiety about access and catching up versus anxiety about the consequences of being at the frontier.

r001.rationale: The response mentions compute access as one immediate concern, alongside keeping up and building a sustainable business, but does not identify insufficient compute as the primary source of anxiety.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Chinese labs’ emphasis on access and catching up with the prominent U.S. focus on AI’s consequences, while acknowledging the distinction is not absolute.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention U.S. CEOs’ unemployment predictions or their effect on American views of AI.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention developers defining AGI by whether it can replace them in their own jobs.

r005.rationale: The response says Chinese labs move quickly under constraints, but does not characterize their attitude as building AI first and seeing what happens afterward.
